title: Quas Primas
opening: Why does the Catholic Church call Jesus the King of the Universe? And why did a pope, nearly a hundred years ago, decide that the Church needed a special celebration to remind us of His kingship? The answer takes us into history, but it also tells us something important about the world we live in today.
body:
There are so many things we do as Catholics without necessarily understanding why. We attend Mass, follow the readings, celebrate feast days, and participate in traditions passed down through generations. But I sometimes wonder how much more meaningful our faith could become if we understood the history behind these celebrations.

Today is the Solemnity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe, commonly called Christ the King Sunday. A solemnity is the highest rank of celebration in the Church's liturgical calendar, reserved for events and mysteries of particular importance to our faith. But this celebration has an especially interesting history.

In 1925, Pope Pius XI established the Feast of Christ the King through his encyclical Quas Primas (which translates to "In the first"). These were the opening words of Pope Pius XI's 1925 ecyclical. Papal encyclicals are traditionally named after their first few words in Latin.  During this time, World War I had ended only seven years earlier. Millions had died, countries were devastated, and Europe was struggling with political instability, nationalism, and growing secularism. People were looking to governments, political movements, and powerful leaders for answers. Pope Pius XI believed society was increasingly pushing God aside and placing its confidence in human power. He wanted to remind Christians that earthly rulers and governments are temporary, but the authority of Christ is eternal.

I find that fascinating because, although a century has passed, how different is our world today? We still look to political leaders to solve our problems. We still divide ourselves over power, wealth, nationality, and beliefs. We still struggle with war, injustice, and the desire to control one another. Perhaps the world hasn't changed as much as we think.

But here's what makes this celebration so extraordinary. When we think of a king, we imagine someone sitting on a throne, surrounded by wealth, authority, and people who serve him. Yet Jesus showed us a completely different kind of king. He washed the feet of His disciples, welcomed sinners, cared for the sick and the poor, and forgave those who hurt Him. Ultimately, He wore a crown of thorns. What kind of king does that? A king whose greatness is revealed through love rather than domination.

Today's readings help us understand this. In Ezekiel, God describes Himself as a shepherd who searches for His lost sheep, brings back those who have wandered, and cares for the injured and weak. Then, in Matthew's Gospel, Jesus describes the final judgment, when the Son of Man separates the sheep from the goats. And what does He ask of us? Did we feed the hungry, welcome the stranger, clothe those in need, care for the sick, and visit those in prison? Jesus tells us that whatever we did for the least among us, we did for Him.

Think about that for a moment. The King of the Universe identifies Himself with the people we so often overlook. He doesn't tell us to seek power or recognition. He asks us to care for one another.

There is another interesting piece of history behind today's celebration. When Pope Pius XI established the feast, it was celebrated on the last Sunday of October. In 1969, during the Church's revision of the liturgical calendar, it was moved to the final Sunday before Advent. Throughout the year, the Church leads us through the life, teachings, suffering, death, and Resurrection of Jesus. At the end, we celebrate Christ as King, looking toward the fulfillment of God's kingdom. Then Advent begins, and we prepare once again for His coming.

The Church's calendar isn't simply a collection of religious holidays. It is designed to help us journey through the mysteries of our faith, year after year, discovering something we may not have understood before.

I think understanding these connections matters. The people who came before us lived through wars, uncertainty, suffering, and tremendous changes in society. They struggled with many of the same questions we face today. When we understand their history, we begin to recognize how our own lives are connected to theirs. Perhaps that understanding can help us approach the future with greater wisdom and faith.

Pope Pius XI wanted the world to remember that Christ's kingdom stands above the powers of this earth. And today's Gospel reminds us what belonging to that kingdom actually looks like. It begins with how we treat one another.

We can honor Jesus with beautiful churches, prayers, celebrations, and traditions. But if we fail to recognize Him in the hungry, the lonely, the sick, or the forgotten, have we really understood what kind of King He is?

Perhaps the greatest way to honor the King of the Universe is to recognize Him in the person standing right in front of us. Give Peace to one another if you attend Mass today, which I strongly encourage. ; )
prayer: Lord Jesus, King of the Universe, thank You for the history, traditions, and teachings that have carried our faith through generations. Help me understand not only what I believe, but why I believe it. Give me the curiosity to learn from those who came before me and the wisdom to carry those lessons into the future. Remind me that Your kingdom is not built on power or wealth, but on love, mercy, and compassion. Open my eyes to recognize You in the people I encounter, especially those who are suffering or forgotten. May my life reflect the kind of King You truly are. Amen.
scripture: Ezekiel 34:11–12, 15–17; Psalm 23:1–3, 5–6; 1 Corinthians 15:20–26, 28; Matthew 25:31–46.  Historical Reference: Pope Pius XI, Quas Primas (1925).
theme: Why the Church celebrates Christ the King, and what a pope living through a troubled world wanted us to understand.
